B.3 Electron beam welding Electron beam welding is a specialized process critical to advanced manufacturing applications across many sectors of importance to the US economy and science including nuclear, aerospace, defense, semi-conductors, Page 20 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program superconducting magnets, and accelerators. Electron beam welding is predominately used to manufacture niobium superconducting accelerators. The DOE has a long history of researching and developing electron beam welding technologies [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. A comprehensive review of the process and its history is provided by Patterson et al. [34]. The considerations and challenges of implementing this critical technology for copper accelerator manufacturing are discussed in the following section. B.3.1 State-of-the-Art Welding of High-Gradient Structures When considering which processes may be best suited for joining copper in accelerator applications both the weldability of the material and the requirements of the application must be considered. Accelerator performance is impacted by microstructure, material purity, geometric tolerances and surface cleanliness especially on the interior surface of the RF structure. Joining processes suitable for completing long- continuous seams will be compared. Solid state processes such as friction stir welding are well suited to work with face-centered-cubic and soft materials like copper. They require a high load perpendicular to the joint, with a high risk deforming the internal RF geometry. In addition, the underbead may have burs or other defects unacceptable for the application, and the process can have limitations with respect to geometry, tool access, and post-weld machining requirements. Friction stir welding has many advantages, including minimal oxidation and ability to join thick-section components, and has been used with great economical success for spent nuclear fuel canisters made from copper [35]. While successful for welding low thermal conductivity metals such as steel, tungsten inert gas (TIG) and metal inert gas (MIG) arc welding processes encounter difficulty when trying to maintain a stable weld pool in high conductivity metals like copper. Welds made from these processes can result in high distortion of the components from shrinkage and thermal gradients as well as significant oxidation. High power density laser beam processes can overcome the limitations encountered by arc processes but the high reflectivity of copper at standard laser wavelengths (1µm or 10µm) results in less than 2% of the laser power being absorbed in the solid state. The absorption of the laser dramatically increases once liquid is formed and increases again once a keyhole vapor column is formed in the liquid.
